manuscript_title: Land sale to a Spaniard, Santiago Xochac (Coyoacan region), 1573
geographic_context: Coyoacan region, central Mexico; Santiago Xochac
language_variety: Sixteenth-century central Mexican Nahuatl (Classical-period candidate; not expert adjudicated)
archive: Archivo General de la Nación (Mexico), Tierras 1735, exp. 2, folio 122
manuscript_page: folio 122, manuscript's sole folio represented as ENL BC16a000
edition_reference: Arthur J. O. Anderson, Frances Berdan, and James Lockhart (eds.), Beyond the Codices (1976), document 16, pp. 98–101; ENL transcription and English translation from James Lockhart papers
source_identity_status: confirmed from ENL description and facsimile

image_inspection.observed_page_structure: one handwritten legal-document page with upper text block and lower signatures/attestation
image_inspection.limitation: Facsimile was inspected in a small web raster. The full text has not been independently deciphered, letter-by-letter collated, or checked against a high-resolution scan.
image_inspection.excerpt_basis: short string located by comparison to ENL's edited analytic transcription; NOT an independent paleographic transcript
image_inspection.excerpt_verification: Verbatim agreement with Lockhart's editorial transcription on ENL; not independently collated to a legible manuscript facsimile. The overbar is retained and an expansion is offered only as an explicitly labeled hypothesis.
token_ambiguities: y¯: overbar likely abbreviates a final nasal and the unit likely represents yn / in; this is a sourced editorial expansion, not an independently checked manuscript glyph
ticnamaca: written ti- can be 2sg or 1pl; final plural -h is absent from editorial spelling; preceding tehuātin and two named sellers support a 1pl contextual interpretation
totlal: source-backed to- 'our' and tlal- 'land' segmentation; exclude the free-citation absolutive -li

knowledge_contamination.reason: ENL's editorial transcription and Lockhart's published translation were consulted to locate and understand the manuscript. Future scoring by us on this same page would not be genuinely blind.

possible_functions: ti-: 1st-person plural 'we' or 2nd-person singular 'you'; surface alone ambiguous
c-: third-person singular object index, roughly 'it'
The 1pl reading is favored by preceding tehuātin ('we') and two named sellers
provisional_morphological_observations.uncertainty: The 1pl suffix -h expected in a fuller present-tense analysis is not visibly written. Colonial spelling frequently omits this sound. Thus exact person is NOT proven by ticnamaca alone. The title and clause are externally edited, not independently collated from the facsimile.
provisional_morphological_observations.assessment: Source-crosschecked morphological decomposition; 1pl subject is context-supported, not form-only proved.

possible_functions: Likely represents yn / in: article-like noun-phrase introductory particle
Overbar in colonial Nahuatl can represent an omitted nasal consonant; not a vowel-length mark here
Keep the editorial source exactly as y¯ and expand only in a separate suggestion
provisional_morphological_observations.uncertainty: A nasal-abbreviation reading is supported by published paleographic work. However no high-resolution independent check confirms the manuscript's specific overbar or exclusion of alternatives.
provisional_morphological_observations.assessment: High-confidence historical scribal convention plus context; expansion is editorial/inferred, not a second attested source spelling.

possible_functions: tlal: possessed land base related to free citation form tlalli
The exact written string totlal is also independently recorded in 1563 central Mexican land-ownership evidence
provisional_morphological_observations.uncertainty: Strong external support for segmentation and possessive interpretation; precise original graphemes and vowel quantity remain uncollated. Do not silently insert a source-unwritten absolutive suffix or editorial macrons.
provisional_morphological_observations.assessment: Strong externally cross-checked possessive parse with independent sixteenth-century attestation of the exact form.

source_crosschecked_morphology.original_transcription_basis: James Lockhart's published analytic transcription, ENL folio a; glyphs not independently deciphered
source_crosschecked_morphology.grammatical_reading: In the edited context: a first-person-plural seller acts on the land owned collectively. A single-token person reading is unresolved; the particle expansion is editorial.
source_crosschecked_morphology.english_reference_kind: Brief contextual paraphrase after Lockhart's published English; not independent translation gold

evidence.basis: Independent Classical Nahuatl subject-prefix table: ti- indexes 1pl or 2sg.
Independent tehuantin 'we'; preceding tehuātin in the same 1573 document supports 1pl context.

claims.unresolved: No final -h plural marker is printed in the edited ticnamaca; it may be historically omitted.

evidence.basis: Independent grammatical object prefix table c-/qui- for third-person singular.

claims.unresolved: Coreference with totlal is inferred from the local phrase, not manually verified from the autograph.

evidence.basis: Molina 1571 II f. 62v and Karttunen 1992 p. 158 establish namaca as a transitive verb 'sell something'.

claims.unresolved: Written stress/vowel length and 1pl -h omission remain unverified for this witness.

claims.role: Historical scribal nasal abbreviation; proposed particle yn/in

evidence.basis: Horn and Lockhart, Mundane Documents in Nahuatl, printed p. 16: original overbars can represent an omitted n or m; preserving the mark is methodologically important.
The in/yn article-like particle is documented in Molina, Karttunen and Lockhart, with yn as historical spelling.

claims.unresolved: Do not rewrite written y¯ as yn in the transcript or treat the overbar as a vowel-length diacritic.

evidence.basis: Independent Classical Nahuatl possessive-prefix table identifies to- 'our'.
Molina 1571 II f. 124r and Karttunen identify tlalli as land/parcel; distinct lexical citation form.
UNAM Gran Diccionario Náhuatl lists exact totlal 'our land' in a separate 1563 central Mexican ownership petition; the possessed tlal base is also catalogued.

claims.unresolved: Does not license blindly generating every possessed-noun form from tlalli.

contextual_evidence.basis: Edited 1573 BC16 text has preceding tehuātin and names two sellers; Lockhart interprets their action as first-person plural selling.
Independent dictionary chane, pl. chaneque supports the nearby tichanneque context as plural residents.
